title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 224 (Actions to be taken in pursuance of inspector’s report)

content.overview: Section 224 provides that if, from any report made under section 223, it appears to the Central Government that any person has been guilty of any offence for which he is criminally liable, the Central Government may prosecute such person for the offence. If it appears that it is expedient that the company should be wound up, the Central Government may present a petition for winding up. If it appears that proceedings ought to be brought in the name of the company for recovery of damages or property, the Central Government may itself bring such proceedings in the name of the company. The section converts the inspector’s report into a basis for prosecution, winding-up or recovery action; it does not replace the need to prove the offence or the civil claim.
content.glance: On inspector’s report (s. 223): CG may prosecute for criminal offences; may present winding-up petition; may bring recovery proceedings in the company’s name; report is a basis for action, not a substitute for proof.
content.study: If from any report made under section 223 it appears to the Central Government that any person has been guilty of any offence for which he is criminally liable, the Central Government may prosecute such person for the offence. If it appears that it is expedient that the company should be wound up, the Central Government may, unless the company is already being wound up, present a petition for winding up. If it appears that any proceedings ought in the public interest to be brought by the company for the recovery of damages or for the recovery of any property, the Central Government may itself bring such proceedings in the name of the company. Current-law framing: start from the s. 223 report; identify the path — prosecution, winding-up petition, or recovery in the company’s name; note that the report supports action but does not itself prove the offence or the civil claim.

sections.heading: Prosecution
sections.body: If the report shows criminal liability, the Central Government may prosecute the person for the offence.

sections.heading: Winding Up
sections.body: If expedient that the company be wound up, CG may present a winding-up petition (unless already being wound up).

sections.heading: Recovery in Company’s Name
sections.body: If recovery of damages or property ought to be brought in the public interest, CG may itself bring proceedings in the name of the company.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: The report is a basis for action; the offence or civil claim must still be proved in the appropriate forum.

provisions.title: Actions to be taken in pursuance of inspector’s report

examples.title: Prosecution on report
examples.body: The inspector’s final report under s. 223 indicates that a director has committed an offence under the Act. The Central Government may prosecute under s. 224.

examples.title: Recovery in company’s name
examples.body: The report shows that property was diverted from the company. CG may bring recovery proceedings in the name of the company under s. 224 without waiting for the board to act.

hypotheticals.question: Does a s. 224 decision to prosecute mean the accused is already convicted?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 224 authorises the Central Government to prosecute on the basis of the report. Guilt must still be established in the criminal court. The report is a basis for launching action, not a substitute for proof.

distinctions.title: Actions on report (s. 224) vs inspector’s report (s. 223)
distinctions.left: CG’s power to prosecute, seek winding up, or recover in company’s name
distinctions.right: Inspector’s duty to submit interim and final reports to CG

misconceptions.trap: The inspector’s report under s. 223 automatically winds up the company and convicts the officers.
misconceptions.correction: Section 224 allows the Central Government to prosecute, present a winding-up petition, or bring recovery proceedings. Each of those steps still requires the normal process of proof and adjudication.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 224 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Confirm s. 223 report. II. Identify path (prosecute / wind up / recover). III. Note that proof is still required. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Report contents; action sought; proof path; precise relief.
